entries.title: make the pipelined pool's seats-freed-together check deterministic
entries.body:
Section 13 of tests/link/std_postgres_async_pipeline failed about once
in 80 runs under load. It printed "over 8 loop turns" where the bound is 5.
The cause was in the async Postgres pool, not in the test.

Every seat waiting for its turn on a connection waited on one shared
wake. Epoll woke those waiters in the order they last waited, which was
often the reverse of answer order. The seat whose turn had come ran last,
so seats freed together were taken one per loop turn.

Each seat now waits on its own turn lane, `seat % 128`. Any event that
leaves a turn come rings the lanes of the waiting seats in answer order:
a done, skip, abandon or doom. On Linux, epoll returns distinct
descriptors in the order they became ready, so the chain completes in
one loop turn there. kqueue promises no order, and there a seat that
runs early re-parks.

A pool now holds up to 257 socket pairs: 514 descriptors at size 8 or
more, 290 at size 1. Before, it held 2 × (size + 129) descriptors.
docs/security/postgres.md records the change.

The check's bound, its line in expected.out and the test are unchanged.
Nothing is retried or skipped.

entries.title: propose WP66, C libraries from their headers
entries.body:
A design note for reading a C library's interface from its header instead
of typing every `declare function` by hand. A `nish c-import` subcommand
would run clang on the header and write an ordinary Nish module of
declarations, struct layouts, out-parameter classes and constants, with an
override file for what a header cannot say (ownership, nullability, which
count goes with which buffer). The note measures a prototype on sqlite3.h,
zlib.h, png.h and openssl/sha.h, and orders the language stages that would
bind what is left: opaque classes, fixed-length array fields, buffers paired
by name, callbacks and linking a library from a package. Its first stage is
the zeroext defect in amritk/nish#1755.

entries.title: measure where a minimal HTTP/1.1 GET spends its instructions and bytes
entries.body:
Measure where a minimal keep-alive GET -> 200 JSON spends its instructions and bytes on Http1Server, to decide whether an opt-in lean Http1Config mode (request line, a few named fields, Content-Length bodies only) is worth building. entries.title: profile-guided builds with nish --link --pgo-generate and --pgo-use
entries.body:
`nish --link` now takes the profile-guided build that only
scripts/build.sh offered before. `--pgo-generate` links an instrumented
binary. Running it writes `.profraw` files, `llvm-profdata merge` turns
them into a profile, and `--pgo-use <profdata>` optimises with that
profile. Both flags reach the program, every runtime unit and the
vendored SQLite, which is most of an SQLite-heavy program's user-space
CPU.

A PGO link bypasses the run cache entirely: it reads and writes no
runtime, SQLite or module entry, so instrumented and plain objects never
mix. The profile path is made absolute before it reaches build.sh, which
compiles SQLite from runtime/sqlite/. Both flags need llvm-profdata on
PATH. When it is missing, the link fails with exit 3 (NL0002 under
--json), names the tool, and links nothing. `--pgo-use` also checks the
file with `llvm-profdata show`, so a raw `.profraw` or a profile from
another LLVM is refused up front.

The following are refused with exit 2 and one line, before anything is
written:
- either flag without --link;
- both flags together;
- an empty, missing, unreadable or non-regular profile (a FIFO, a
  device or a directory);
- `--profile debug` or `wasi`;
- a non-host --target;
- `nish run`.

The user guide's CLI page gains "Optimizing a build", which shows the
three-step flow.

entries.title: read SQLite tables and indexes through B-tree cursors
entries.body:
`nish/sqlite` gains a `Cursor`. It walks one table or index through SQLite's own B-tree, without preparing or stepping a statement, for hot reads a program plans by hand, such as a feed that walks an index and looks rows up by rowid.

- **Transactions.** `Database.beginRead()` and `endRead()` bracket a read transaction.
- **Opening a cursor.** `openCursor(name, columns)` opens a cursor on a table or index. It checks the declared column list against the schema and refuses a mismatch, a view, a virtual table, a `WITHOUT ROWID` table, a generated column, an expression index or a non-BINARY index with `SQLITE_SCHEMA`.
- **Moving.** `first`, `last`, `next`, `previous`, `seekRowid`, and `seek` on an integer or text key prefix (`SEEK_GE`, `SEEK_GT`, `SEEK_LE`, `SEEK_LT`).
- **Reading.** `rowid`, `columnI64`, `columnType` and `columnInto`. Every row call answers a scalar and allocates nothing.
- **Invalidation.** Any `exec`, a statement that is not a plain read, a commit or rollback, `endRead` and `close` invalidate every cursor on the connection before they run. An invalidated cursor answers `SQLITE_MISUSE`.

SQLite stays unmodified at 3.54.1. Its B-tree and record functions are static in the amalgamation, so `runtime/sqlite/nish-sqlite.c` now includes `sqlite3.c` and is compiled as one native unit; `sqlite3.c` is no longer compiled on its own. The adapter writes no `BtCursor` field and reads neither the file format nor the record format by hand.

The runtime size gate now measures the adapter as what its unit adds over `sqlite3.c`, compiled with `scripts/build.sh`'s SQLite options. The design, with link-time costs before and after, is in `docs/sqlite-cursor.md`, and the security record covers raw record reads.

entries.title: accept optional chaining and nullish coalescing under --compat
entries.body:
WP28 C1, first stage. Under `--compat`, two dialect features admit forms that strict Nish refuses, each keeping Node's meaning:

- optional-chaining: a statement `a?.b`, `a?.[i]…` or `a?.m(args)` compiles to a null test that skips the rest of the statement, arguments included, from the first null link. An element read the chain would carry past the end of an array (a final `?.[i]`, `a?.xs[i];`, `xs[i]?.m();`, parenthesised or not) stays refused in both dialects with NL1067, because Node answers `undefined` where Nish's bounds check panics. An optional call `f?.()` stays refused (NL1068).
- nullish: a `??` whose left operand can never be missing (a documented allowlist of forms) compiles to its left operand, with the NL9021 performance warning naming the default to drop.

Each strict refusal that a feature would admit names the feature to add to `nish.compat`. For a program the strict dialect accepts, a strict build is unchanged, `--emit-ts` included.
entries.author: Redis Stasa

entries.title: accept string switch and for...of over a string under --compat
entries.body:
WP28 C1, second stage. Two more `--compat` dialect features, each matching Node:

- string-switch: a `switch` on a string whose labels are string literals, templates with no substitution, or module `const` strings compiles to a `nish_str_eq` chain in source order. Fallthrough, a `default` in the middle, `break` and labelled `break` behave as in Node. A duplicate label (compared by cooked text) and a non-constant label (NL2799) are refused.
- for-of-string: `for...of` over a string binds one code point per pass, as a fresh string of its UTF-8 bytes. A pass takes the lead byte and only the continuation bytes that follow it, so invalid UTF-8 takes Node's number of passes. The escape analysis treats each code point as an allocation, so a scoped arena pass never frees one kept past the loop.

Each strict refusal names the feature to add to `nish.compat`. For a program the strict dialect accepts, a strict build is unchanged.

entries.title: A package links a C library or its own C sources
entries.body:
A package's package.json can now name what it links: `"nish": { "link": { "libraries": [...], "sources": [...] } }`. `nish run` and `--link` pass each library as `-l<name>` and compile each C source beside the runtime, with no hand-run scripts/build.sh. A dependency's link takes effect only when the root package grants it under `nish.link.dependencies.<name>`; an ungranted entry is NL3061.

The manifest reader fails closed: an unknown key, a repeated key or package, a value of the wrong shape, or an entry that is not printable ASCII is refused (NL3059, NL3060) rather than ignored, and a library name or source path cannot become a flag or leave its package (checked again by scripts/build.sh). The `nish run` cache keys the link set, each source's bytes and every file `clang -M` lists for it. The accepted limits are recorded: `.incbin` files, a later shadowing header, and a static library's own bytes are not keyed. SQLite's built-in link stays a LinkSet flag. The security record is docs/security/package-link.md.

Part of WP66 (S7). Tests: tests/link/pkg_link_*, tests/run.js package-link

entries.title: cache checked cursor shapes and keep read-transaction statements prepared

* perf(runtime): cache checked cursor shapes and keep read-transaction statements prepared

openCursor re-ran its schema check (seven pragma and schema queries) on
every open, and beginRead/endRead parsed BEGIN, a schema read and COMMIT
on every call, so one read transaction per request cost about 12x a
prepared SQL statement. A connection now keeps up to eight checked shapes,
answered only inside a SQLITE_TXN_READ transaction under the same schema
cookie, and prepares its BEGIN, schema read and COMMIT once.

A link program checks that a kept cursor shape is answered again and is
refused after ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN, a DROP and CREATE, another
connection's change, and a rolled-back write transaction matched by as many
committed DDL statements; that more shapes than the cache keeps each read
right; and, rerun under -DSQLITE_DEBUG, that close frees the kept KeyInfo
under the connection's mutex. The cursor design note and the SQLite security
record describe the cache's validity rule and the kept statements.

entries.title: pair a C buffer with its count by name, at any unsigned width
entries.body: An interop declaration can now name the parameter that carries a buffer's length, and that count may be a `u8`, `u16`, `u32` or `u64`, or a field of an out class (zlib's `uLongf *destLen`). A buffer whose length does not fit a narrower count is refused at the call before C runs, and the prover removes the check where the count is the buffer's own length. WP53's adjacent-`u64` rule compiles unchanged.
entries.author: Redis Stasa

entries.title: fixed-length array fields in a declare class
entries.body: A `declare class` field can now be a C fixed-length array (`unsigned int h[5]` in SHA_CTX, `char sysname[65]` in utsname), laid out inline as `[N x T]` exactly as clang lays it out. An element is read and written by index: a dynamic index takes an unsigned range check, a constant one out of range is a compile-time error, and the prover removes the check where it can show the index in range. The field cannot escape as a Nish array; unions and bitfields stay refused.

entries.title: nish c-import writes a Nish module from a C header
entries.body: `nish c-import` reads a C header through clang and writes a checked-in Nish module of declare functions, declare classes, out classes and constants, using only today's language. An override file adds what the header cannot say (which functions to bind, a parameter's role, a non-null or owned return) and never reaches past the header. Whatever it cannot bind is listed, in header order, in a Not bound block. The module records the target's data model, and a build for another data model is refused with the command that regenerates it.

entries.title: nish c-import emits opaque classes, array fields and named buffer pairs

A buffer whose override names its count becomes `CountedBy<…, "count">`, with the count a `u8` to `u64` by value or an out class C writes back through a pointer.

entries.title: two modules may each keep a private function or generic of one name

entries.title: split lines in std/text sixteen positions at a time

entries.title: add --allow-panics and pass it wherever the repository builds a program that may panic
entries.body:
`nish --allow-panics` undoes an earlier `--deny-panics`. When both flags are given, the last one decides. A package's `"nish".noPanic` list still holds under it. The default does not change yet, so the flag changes no IR and no build outcome on its own. It prepares for holding the root package to no panic by default.

The repository's own builds of programs that may panic on purpose now pass the flag, but only to a compiler whose `--help` lists it. Those builds are the self-build stages, the test corpus, the tests/link programs, the Nish-written harnesses, bench drivers, CI workflows and the interop image. One probing helper per language decides this: `scripts/nish-compiler.sh` (`nish_allow_panics`) and `tests/allow-panics.js`. A seed that predates the flag is never passed it, and the helpers can go once every supported seed accepts it. Builds a user would copy, under examples/ and docs/, stay strict. A tests/run.js check fails on a raw compile that bypasses the helper.

entries.title: keep each test shard's results in the step summary
entries.body:

entries.title: read named constants, masks, charCodeAt and down-counting loops in the panic prover
entries.body:
--deny-panics now proves four kinds of correct code it used to refuse, and drops their runtime checks from the IR:

- A module- or function-level `const` bound to an integer literal, a folded constant, or a conversion of a literal that fits (`toU64(0)`, `toU8(200)`) is read as its value, as a `new Array` length, a divisor, a mask or shift, or the zero in `b === zero ? a : a % b`. A `let`, a field, a call result, a conversion that wraps and a negative length stay refused.
- `x & C` is read as `[0, C]` and `x >>> k` as `[0, 2^(bits-k) - 1]`; `toI32` of a `u32` whose range fits keeps that range.
- `s.charCodeAt(i)` is read as `[0, 255]`, the byte it answers natively and under --emit-ts, and `Math.clz32(x)` as `[0, 32]`.
- A loop counter that starts at a string's length and is only decremented keeps that upper bound, so `t.charCodeAt(end - 1)` under `end > 0` needs no index check, as long as nothing else writes the counter or reassigns the string.

In vector, NL2458 refusals that land in std fall from 701 to 580; the Map probe overflow, `trimEnd`'s index and both `INITIAL_SLOTS` array lengths no longer refuse. docs/LANGUAGE.md's "Panic sites" lists what each proof now reads.

entries.title: hold the root package to no panic by default; --allow-panics relaxes it
entries.body:
BREAKING CHANGE: a build is now held to no panic by default. Without a flag, every module of the root package may keep no panic site except running out of memory. An unproven index, an unproven overflow, or a call that can exit is refused at compile time (NL2457, NL2458), and `nish run`, `--emit-ts` and `--compat` are held to it too. `--allow-panics` relaxes this. Under it, the scope is exactly the modules the package's `"nish".noPanic` list names, so a committed `noPanic` list still holds under the flag. No manifest value relaxes the default: an empty list and a missing key change nothing. `--deny-panics` spells out the default. When both flags are given, the last one wins. `--emit-ast` skips the default check but still refuses an explicit `--deny-panics`.

std/ is not panic-free yet, so a strict module cannot yet call `Map`, `Set`, `split` or the JSON reads. Each reaches a panic site in std/ that no caller can remove. A program that needs them builds with `--allow-panics` until std/ migrates. The examples that do so say why in their first lines and show the flag in their build commands. Guide pages whose examples need the flag say so on the page.

To migrate a project such as amritk/vector, add `--allow-panics` to its build, list modules in `noPanic` one at a time as they become panic-free, and drop the flag once every module is listed. On amritk/vector, the new default refused 2,459 sites on 2,065 lines in 92 files, measured before the prover improvements of #1999.

Measured: recording panic sites on src/compile.ts (--allow-panics with --emit-panics against --allow-panics alone, 7 interleaved pairs, 4 cores) costs +0.08 s on 2.43 s, +3.5% by medians; per pair -0.2% to +7.6%, unrecorded runs spread 2.37-2.50 s (±2.7%); an upper bound, since it includes writing the 3.5 MB listing
Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md#panic-sites
Tests: tests/link/no_panic_default, tests/link/no_panic_empty_list, tests/link/allow_panics_relaxed, node tests/run.js allow-panics

Part of #1847.
